\chapter{Five Things a Form Asks For}
\label{ch:el-ordenador-y-el-correo-electronico}
\hlchaptermodality{393}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say el ordenador, internet, el correo electrónico, la dirección and la nacionalidad, and name five things I need to fill in a form online.}

Complete ES-C393-nacionalidad: name five things I need to fill in a form online, and say one thing about each.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[el ordenador]{el ordenador — the word stayed, the meaning arrived}

\label{lesson:ES-C393-ordenador}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the passenger}, then \emph{August}. (\emph{El pasajero}; \emph{agosto}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item escribir — what you do at one.
  \item la oficina — where you will most often see one.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{or-de-na-DOR}, four beats with the weight on the last. Both \emph{d}s are soft, closer to the \emph{th} of English \emph{this} than to a hard \emph{d}, because a vowel runs into each of them. The two \emph{r}s are single taps, not rolls. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el ordenador} — a computer.

Latin \textbf{ōrdinātor} was an agent noun — a \emph{-tor} word, the one who does the thing — built on \textbf{ōrdināre}, and behind that on \textbf{ōrdō, ōrdinem}: a rank, a row, things put in their proper places. So the word says \emph{the one who puts in order}, and English carries the same Latin in \textbf{ordain}, \textbf{ordinal}, \textbf{order}, \textbf{coordinate} and \textbf{subordinate}.

Now the careful part, because two different things happened at two different times and running them together is the mistake.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item The \textbf{word} \emph{ordenador}, \textquotedblleft{}one who orders or arranges\textquotedblright{}, is old in Spanish and came down from that Latin.
  \item The \textbf{computing sense} was taken from French \textbf{ordinateur}.
\end{itemize}

Spanish already owned the shape and imported only the meaning. Nothing was borrowed letter by letter, and nothing was translated piece by piece; a sense moved across and settled into a word that was standing there waiting.

The French side has two dates, both defensible, so say which one you mean. The coinage appears in a \textbf{letter of 16 April 1955}, written for IBM France, who thought \emph{calculateur} too narrow for the machine. The CNRTL dates the computing sense to \textbf{1956} — the first use actually recorded.

One caution before you take it travelling. The Academy's dictionary marks the computing sense \textbf{Esp.}, for Spain. Across much of Latin America the machine goes by \emph{computadora} or \emph{computador}, so \emph{ordenador} names it in Madrid and marks you as speaking Peninsular Spanish in Lima.

\begin{quote}
\emph{el ordenador nuevo} — the new computer.
\end{quote}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can name the machine you fill forms in on: \emph{el ordenador}. And you can tell a borrowed word from a borrowed meaning.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el ordenador}
  \item \emph{un ordenador nuevo}
  \item \emph{el pasajero tiene un ordenador}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{ōrdinātor} name in Latin? (The one who puts things in order.) And which of the two — the word or the machine sense — came from French? (The machine sense; the word was already Spanish.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[internet]{internet — the same letters, a different beat}

\label{lesson:ES-C393-internet}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{August}, then \emph{the computer}. (\emph{Agosto}; \emph{el ordenador}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el ordenador — what you reach it from.
  \item el teléfono — the other thing you reach it from.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{in-ter-NET}, three beats with the weight on the last. The \emph{t}s are dental, the tongue touching the back of the top teeth rather than the ridge behind them. The \emph{r} is one tap. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{internet} — the internet.

It came into Spanish out of English with nothing changed on the page. The English word is a hybrid, and the two halves come from opposite ends of Europe:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{inter-} is Latin \textbf{inter}, \textquotedblleft{}between\textquotedblright{} — the same piece inside \emph{international} and \emph{intervene};
  \item \textbf{net} is Germanic, Old English \textbf{nett}, a mesh of knotted cord.
\end{itemize}

A Latin prefix welded to a Germanic noun, in a coinage of the last century.

The page is unchanged; the sound is not, and this is the thing worth carrying away. English puts the weight at the front: \emph{ÍN-ter-net}. Spanish puts it at the back: \textbf{in-ter-NET}. The Academy's \emph{Diccionario panhispánico de dudas} spells this out. An English speaker who keeps the English beat will be understood and will sound foreign for exactly one syllable's worth of reason.

The same dictionary is candid about the article, which is unsettled. Both \emph{el internet} and \emph{la internet} are recorded, and the \textbf{feminine is the more frequent} of the two — the pull coming from \emph{red}, the Spanish word for a net, which is feminine. So the word is drifting toward the gender of its own translation.

Two more things it records. Written with a capital when it names the one global network; written small when the word works as an ordinary noun. And the shape resists two temptations: no \emph{internete} with a vowel tacked on to make it comfortable, and no tilde anywhere on it.

\begin{quote}
\emph{todo está en internet} — it is all on the internet.
\end{quote}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can say \emph{internet} with the Spanish beat, and you know why the article wobbles.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{internet}
  \item \emph{el ordenador tiene internet}
  \item \emph{en agosto no tengo internet}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which syllable carries the weight in Spanish? (The last: \emph{in-ter-NET}.) And which article does the Academy record as the more frequent, and why? (The feminine, pulled there by \emph{red}, which is feminine.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el correo electrónico]{el correo electrónico — the messenger who only looks like a runner}

\label{lesson:ES-C393-correo-electronico}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the computer}, then \emph{the internet}. (\emph{El ordenador}; \emph{internet}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la carta — what it replaced.
  \item internet — what it travels over.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{co-RRE-o e-lec-TRÓ-ni-co}. The \emph{rr} is rolled, held longer than a single tap. Every \emph{c} here comes out as a hard \emph{k}, each standing before an \emph{o} or a consonant. \emph{Correo} takes its weight on the middle beat; the written accent marks where \emph{electrónico} takes its own. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el correo electrónico} — email.

\emph{Correo} sits one letter from \textbf{correr}, \textquotedblleft{}to run\textquotedblright{}, and a messenger runs, so the story writes itself. The story is wrong, and that is the point of this word.

The Academy's dictionary gives the road. Spanish \textbf{correo} comes from Catalan \textbf{correu}, and Catalan took it from Old French \textbf{corlieu}, \textquotedblleft{}a messenger\textquotedblright{} — a compound of a verb meaning \emph{to run} plus \textbf{lieu}, \textquotedblleft{}place\textquotedblright{}. Catalan then reshaped it under the pull of its own \emph{córrer}.

So Latin \textbf{currere}, \textquotedblleft{}to run\textquotedblright{}, really is the ancestor of that first element. But \emph{correo} was not built in Spanish out of \emph{correr}, and part of the resemblance is a later tidying-up rather than descent. Right about the ancestor, wrong about the route.

Now the best thing in the word. That same Old French \emph{courlieu} gave English a bird: the \textbf{curlew}. Etymonline says the bird's name imitates its cry — and that it was \textquotedblleft{}apparently assimilated with \emph{corliu}, 'runner, messenger'\textquotedblright{}. Two unrelated ancestries, a call heard on a marsh and a word for a courier, walked into Old French and came out wearing one shape.

From \emph{currere}, English keeps \textbf{current}, \textbf{courier}, \textbf{course}, \textbf{corridor}, \textbf{occur} and \textbf{excursion}.

The second half is far younger. \emph{Electrónico} is \emph{electrón} plus \emph{-ico}, and \emph{electrón} goes back to Ancient Greek \textbf{ēlektron}, \textquotedblleft{}amber\textquotedblright{}. A modern international scientific word, passed between languages rather than handed down inside one.

Put the halves together and you have a loan translation of English \emph{electronic mail}, element for element. The Academy recommends the full form and turns down \emph{correo-e}.

One ambiguity to expect: \emph{correo} alone now carries the email sense in ordinary speech, so it can mean the post or the inbox.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can name the thing a form asks for: \emph{el correo electrónico}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el correo electrónico}
  \item \emph{mi correo electrónico}
  \item \emph{leo el correo electrónico en el ordenador}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Did \emph{correo} grow out of \emph{correr}? (No — it came through Catalan \emph{correu} from Old French \emph{corlieu}, a messenger, and \emph{córrer} only reshaped it afterwards.) Which English bird shares that word? (The curlew.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la dirección]{la dirección — the word for where you live}

\label{lesson:ES-C393-direccion}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the internet}, then \emph{email}. (\emph{Internet}; \emph{el correo electrónico}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la calle — the first line of one.
  \item el número — the second line of one.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{di-rec-CIÓN}, three beats with the weight on the last, where the written accent puts it. The double \emph{cc} is two different sounds in a row: a hard \emph{k}, then a soft \emph{c} before the \emph{i}, an \emph{s} across the Americas and a \emph{th} across much of Spain. The \emph{r} is a single tap. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la dirección} — an address.

Behind it is Latin \textbf{dīrēctiō, dīrēctiōnem}. What is worth seeing is that this word did not come down to Spanish through everyday speech; it was lifted out of written Latin, later and deliberately. You do not have to take that on trust, because Spanish kept both outcomes side by side, twice over.

Look at what happened to Latin \textbf{dīrēctus}:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{derecho} — \textquotedblleft{}right, straight\textquotedblright{};
  \item \textbf{directo} — \textquotedblleft{}direct\textquotedblright{}.
\end{itemize}

And at what happened to Latin \textbf{ratiōnem}:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{razón} — \textquotedblleft{}reason\textquotedblright{};
  \item \textbf{ración} — \textquotedblleft{}a ration, a portion\textquotedblright{}.
\end{itemize}

Each pair is one Latin word arriving twice. In each pair, one member has been handled by generations of speakers and shows it, and the other still looks close to the Latin it was copied from. Now put our word beside them. Where \emph{derecho} melted its Latin \emph{c} away into \emph{-ch-}, \emph{dirección} still shows that \emph{c}. And it ends \textbf{-ción}, as \emph{ración} does, rather than \textbf{-zón}, as \emph{razón} does. It stands with the copies, not with the worn ones.

The real trap here is the meaning. Spanish \textbf{dirección} covers three things:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the \textbf{address} where you live or receive post;
  \item the \textbf{management} or leadership of a company or a school;
  \item \textbf{direction}, the way something points.
\end{itemize}

English \emph{direction} has only the third. A Spaniard who \emph{trabaja en la dirección} works in management, not in a compass. On a form, the first sense is the one being asked for.

English holds the same Latin in \textbf{direction}, \textbf{direct}, \textbf{dress}, \textbf{address} and \textbf{redress}.

\begin{quote}
\emph{¿Cuál es tu dirección?} — What is your address?
\end{quote}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can give the line of a form that asks where you live: \emph{la dirección}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la dirección}
  \item \emph{mi dirección y mi correo electrónico}
  \item \emph{busco la dirección en internet}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of \emph{derecho} and \emph{directo} does \emph{dirección} resemble, and which of \emph{razón} and \emph{ración}? (\emph{Directo}, and \emph{ración}.) What does \emph{dirección} mean on a form? (The address where you live.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la nacionalidad]{la nacionalidad — a word built at home on a borrowed floor}

\label{lesson:ES-C393-nacionalidad}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{email}, then \emph{the address}. (\emph{El correo electrónico}; \emph{la dirección}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el país — what it names you by.
  \item el apellido — the line above it on the form.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{na-cio-na-li-DAD}, five beats with the weight on the last. The \emph{c} before \emph{i} is soft — an \emph{s} across the Americas, a \emph{th} across much of Spain — and \emph{cio} is one beat, the \emph{i} gliding into the \emph{o}. Both \emph{d}s are soft, the final one barely there. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la nacionalidad} — nationality.

Assembled in Spanish rather than imported: \emph{nacional} plus \textbf{-idad}, the ending that turns a description into the quality itself.

The borrowing sits one floor down, in \textbf{nación}. That came from Latin \textbf{nātiō, nātiōnem}: \emph{a birth}, then \emph{the place of birth}, then \emph{a people}. Corominas dates \emph{nación} to the \textbf{fifteenth century} — late, and lateness is the tell for a word taken from books rather than speakers.

Set it beside \textbf{razón}, \textquotedblleft{}reason\textquotedblright{}, which came down the long way, through mouths. Both Latin ancestors ended alike; the two Spanish words do not. \emph{Razón} has been worn smooth. \emph{Nación} still has its Latin face on.

There is a limit to what can be claimed for the modern political sense. Etymonline notes that English \emph{nationality} is \textquotedblleft{}in some usages perhaps from French \emph{nationalité}\textquotedblright{}, and nineteenth-century French influence on the Spanish sense is plausible — and unsettled. Hold it loosely at the top, firmly at the root.

English relatives run wide: \textbf{nation}, \textbf{native}, \textbf{nature}, \textbf{innate}, and further back \textbf{genus} and \textbf{genesis}.

One more sense exists. In Spain, \emph{nacionalidad} also names an autonomous community whose statute recognises a special historical and cultural identity.

\begin{quote}
\emph{¿Cuál es tu nacionalidad?} — What is your nationality?
\end{quote}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can fill in a form online end to end: the machine, the network, the address that reaches you, the address you live at, and where you are from.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Name the five things you need to fill in a form online, and say one thing about each.

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el ordenador} — \emph{el ordenador es nuevo}
  \item \emph{internet} — \emph{el ordenador tiene internet}
  \item \emph{el correo electrónico} — \emph{mi correo electrónico es corto}
  \item \emph{la dirección} — \emph{mi dirección está en esta calle}
  \item \emph{la nacionalidad} — \emph{mi nacionalidad está en el pasaporte}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Was \emph{nacionalidad} borrowed, or built? (Built in Spanish, from \emph{nacional} plus \emph{-idad}; the borrowing is \emph{nación} underneath it.) And which word shows the other road out of Latin? (\emph{Razón} — worn down by speech, where \emph{nación} was copied from the page.)
\end{tcolorbox}
